title: The steady one
hookLine: Arjuna asks the most practical question in the book: what does a person like that actually look like?
carry: the sthitaprajna feels everything and isn't knocked over
tomorrow: From desire to anger, and the ocean's peace
last: THE DOING IS YOURS, THE FRUIT ISN'T.

lines: THE ONE WHO DOESN'T GO CRAZY.
HOW DO THEY TALK, SIT, WALK?
cards: Some people are like this. A grandmother, a nurse on the night shift, a coach, a friend. When the room goes crazy, they don't.

Bad news comes, and they take it in, and they're still themselves. Good news comes, and they're glad, and still themselves. Arjuna has just heard Krishna talk about evenness, about acting with open hands.
So he asks the obvious question. What does such a person look like? How do they talk?
How do they sit? How do they walk?

teach.b: In Sanskrit, Arjuna's question begins: sthitaprajnasya ka bhasha. What is the description of the one whose wisdom is steady? Sthita, standing firm.
Prajna, wisdom. Krishna's answer isn't a list of rules. It's a portrait.
When someone lets go of all the cravings that swirl in the mind, and is content in the self, by the self, that one is steady. Then the heart of it: duhkheshv anudvigna manah, sukheshu vigata sprihah.

teach.h: UNSHAKEN IN SORROW, UNCRAVING IN JOY.
teach.b: The one whose mind isn't shaken in sorrow, who doesn't crave in pleasure, free from clinging, fear and anger: that's a sage of steady mind. Not someone who feels nothing. Someone who isn't knocked over.

Like a tortoise drawing in its limbs from every side, the steady one can draw the senses back from the things that pull at them. The tortoise still has legs, and uses them. It just isn't dragged around by them.
Then Krishna says something honest. If you just stop eating, the objects of the senses fall away, but the taste for them stays.

teach.h: THE TASTE STAYS. SEE SOMETHING HIGHER.
teach.b: Only when a person sees something higher does even the taste go.
And the senses are strong: they can carry off the mind of even a wise person who's trying. So sit, he says, with your mind on me. This isn't willpower alone.
These verses meant a great deal to Gandhi, who had them recited at the prayer meetings in his ashram: a portrait to measure yourself by, gently, every evening.

how: The verses on the sthitaprajna, the one of steady wisdom (Gita 2.54–2.72), are recited daily in some Hindu homes, and were recited at the prayer meetings in Gandhi's ashram.

o: a hermit living in a forest

games.q: what's inside the portrait — tap the pairs.
p: draws in its limbs from every side
stays, until something higher is seen

s: the steady one isn't shaken in sorrow or craving in joy. still feeling, not knocked over.
the Gita admits the senses can carry off even a wise mind
so Krishna says: sit with your mind on me. it isn't willpower alone.
Gandhi had these verses recited in his ashram
at the prayer meetings, as a portrait to measure oneself by.

games.q: bad news arrives for the steady one of the Gita, the sthitaprajna. what happens?
o: nothing. they've trained themselves to feel nothing.
they feel it, and aren't knocked over.
they run to the forest so news can't reach them.
games.why: unshaken in sorrow, uncraving in joy (2.56). not someone who feels nothing: someone who isn't knocked over, and still walks through the world.

practice: Notice everything pulling at your senses: sounds, the phone nearby, an itch, a smell from the kitchen.
Then, like a tortoise drawing in its legs, gently draw your attention back to the breath, hearing but not reaching toward sounds, feeling but not chasing sensations, and rest there, shell and all.
When something pulls you out, and it will, don't be annoyed; just draw in again.

wordCard.voice: Sthitaprajna. The one whose wisdom is steady: unshaken in sorrow, uncraving in joy, drawing in the senses like a tortoise.

orig.note: Sanskrit: sthita, standing firm, and prajna, wisdom. the one whose wisdom is steady.
